summary: Tantalum-based superconducting qubits exhibit quasiparticle tunneling rates approximately three times higher than niobium qubits (1542 Hz vs 461 Hz), with stronger dependence on infrared radiation power ($\Gamma_0 \propto P_W^{2.6 ± 0.1}$ for Ta vs $P_W^{1.4 ± 0.1}$ for Nb), but infrared filtering reduces tantalum tunneling rates to 300 Hz and niobium to 100 Hz. The time-dependent decay of tunneling rates over days after cooldown indicates slowly radiating components in the cryostat contribute significantly to quasiparticle generation in both materials.
motivation: Tantalum films reduce dielectric losses and extend qubit coherence times compared to niobium, but the material choice also influences sensitivity to quasiparticle-induced decoherence, motivating investigation of whether radiative backgrounds affect these two superconducting platforms differently.
method: Quasiparticle tunneling rates were extracted via charge-parity mapping on offset-charge-sensitive transmons ($E_J/E_C \approx 20$, charge dispersion $\approx 5$ MHz) using a Ramsey-type protocol repeated at 0.5–1 MHz. Power spectral density analysis of parity time traces identified tunneling rates as the characteristic switching frequency. Tantalum and niobium qubits with Al/AlO$_x$/Al junctions were exposed to thermal radiation from a Manganin wire (2 Ω, 0.2 mm diameter) and characterized with various combinations of in-line Eccosorb filters and foam absorbers.
result: With baseline filtering, tantalum showed $\Gamma_0 = (1542 ± 176)$ Hz vs niobium $(461 ± 16)$ Hz; foam absorbers alone reduced rates by factors of 11.9 (Ta) and 6.8 (Nb), while combined foam + in-line filters achieved $(300 ± \text{?})$ Hz (Ta) and $(100 ± \text{?})$ Hz (Nb). Tunneling rates decayed as power laws $\propto t^{-0.73}$ (Ta) and $t^{-0.55}$ (Nb) over 2–3 weeks post-cooldown, consistent with slow thermal radiation from internal components.
